title: Area and Volume, Part 2: Medium and Hard Problems

beats.say: In part one, we found the volume and surface area of a box, and we saw that cones and pyramids hold one third of the matching prism.

card.text: Cone = one third of the cylinder

beats.say: In this video, we use scaling, and then solve a hard problem where a cylinder is melted and recast as a cone.
Medium example. A cube has an edge of three centimeters. Every edge is doubled. By what factor does the volume increase?
The tempting answer is two, because the edges doubled. But volume is cubed, so the factor must be two cubed.
The new cube has an edge of six, and the old cube has an edge of three. The ratio of the volumes is six cubed over three cubed.
Six cubed is two hundred sixteen, and three cubed is twenty-seven, so we have the two volumes.
Two hundred sixteen divided by twenty-seven is eight. So the volume increases by a factor of eight, which is two cubed.
Hard example. A solid metal cylinder with a radius of four and a height of nine is melted and recast as a cone with a radius of four. What is the height of the cone?

card.sub: Recast as a cone with r = 4. Find h.

beats.say: The key idea is that melting does not change the amount of metal. So the volume of the cone equals the volume of the cylinder.
The volume of a cylinder is pi r squared times h. We substitute a radius of four and a height of nine.
Four squared is sixteen. So the volume is pi times sixteen times nine.
Sixteen times nine is one hundred forty-four. So the cylinder holds one hundred forty-four pi cubic units of metal.
The volume of a cone is one third pi r squared h. We set this equal to the volume of the cylinder, one hundred forty-four pi.
Four squared is sixteen. So one third times sixteen is sixteen thirds, and the equation is sixteen thirds pi h equals one hundred forty-four pi.
Divide both sides by pi. The pi cancels, because it appears on both sides.
Multiply both sides by three sixteenths, the reciprocal of sixteen thirds. One hundred forty-four times three over sixteen.
One hundred forty-four divided by sixteen is nine, and nine times three is twenty-seven. So the height of the cone is twenty-seven.
Check with a shortcut. With the same base, a cone holds one third as much as a cylinder of the same height. So the cone must be three times as tall as the cylinder. Three times nine is twenty-seven.
To recap. When all lengths are multiplied by k, area is multiplied by k squared, and volume by k cubed.
When a solid is melted and recast, the volume stays the same, so set the two volume formulas equal.
Leave pi in until the end, since it cancels. In the next video, we look at common traps and the fast way with Desmos.
